The Cell
An Illustrated Guide to Important Organelles
Every living cell is a miniature, bustling city — with power plants, factories, shipping departments,
recycling centers, and a command headquarters. This guide walks through the essential
organelles found in eukaryotic cells, pairing a detailed illustration with a clear explanation of
structure and function for each.

Nucleus
The control center of the cell
Structure & Function
•  Surrounded by a double membrane called the
nuclear envelope, studded with nuclear pores.
•  Nuclear pores regulate the movement of molecules
— such as RNA and proteins — into and out of the
nucleus.
•  Contains chromatin (DNA loosely wound around
proteins), which condenses into chromosomes before
cell division.
•  Houses the nucleolus, a dense region where
ribosomal RNA is synthesized and ribosome subunits
are assembled.
•  Directs cellular activity by controlling gene
expression — essentially the instruction manual for the
whole cell.
Quick Facts
•  Largest organelle in most animal cells.
•  Discovered by Robert Brown in 1831.
•  Human cells contain about 2 meters of DNA packed inside a nucleus only ~6 micrometers wide.

Mitochondrion
The powerhouse of the cell
Structure & Function
•  Enclosed by a double membrane: a smooth outer
membrane and a highly folded inner membrane.
•  The folds of the inner membrane, called cristae,
increase surface area for energy production.
•  Site of cellular respiration, converting glucose and
oxygen into usable chemical energy (ATP).
•  Contains its own small circular DNA and ribosomes,
a legacy of its ancient bacterial origins.
•  The fluid-filled interior, or matrix, holds enzymes
needed for the citric acid (Krebs) cycle.
Quick Facts
•  Thought to have originated from ancient free-living bacteria (endosymbiotic theory).
•  Number per cell varies enormously — from a few hundred to several thousand, depending on
energy needs.

•  Muscle and liver cells, which need lots of energy, are especially rich in mitochondria.

Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum
The protein assembly line
Structure & Function
•  A network of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae)
continuous with the nuclear envelope.
•  Studded on its outer surface with ribosomes, giving
it a "rough" appearance.
•  Ribosomes attached here synthesize proteins
destined for secretion, the cell membrane, or other
organelles.
•  Newly made proteins are folded and can be tagged
with carbohydrate chains inside the ER lumen.
•  Proteins are packaged into transport vesicles and
shipped onward to the Golgi apparatus.
Quick Facts
•  Especially abundant in cells that secrete large amounts of protein, such as pancreatic cells.
•  "Rough" refers only to appearance under a microscope — the ribosomes create the studded
texture.

Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum
The lipid and detox workshop
Structure & Function
•  A tubular, interconnected network of membranes
lacking ribosomes — hence "smooth."
•  Main site of lipid and steroid hormone synthesis,
including cholesterol.
•  Plays a key role in detoxifying drugs and harmful
metabolic byproducts, especially in liver cells.
•  Stores and regulates calcium ions, which is
especially important in muscle cells (as the
sarcoplasmic reticulum).
•  Helps package and transport lipids to other parts of
the cell.
Quick Facts
•  Liver cells contain unusually large amounts of smooth ER due to their detox role.
•  In muscle cells, a specialized form controls contraction by releasing calcium.

Golgi Apparatus
The post office of the cell
Structure & Function
•  A stack of flattened, membrane-bound sacs called
cisternae.
•  Receives proteins and lipids from the ER at its "cis"
face and modifies them as they move through.
•  Adds finishing touches such as sugar groups
(glycosylation) and tags proteins for their final
destination.
•  Packages finished products into vesicles that bud off
from the "trans" face for delivery.
•  Also produces lysosomes in animal cells.
Quick Facts
•  Named after Camillo Golgi, who first described it in 1897.
•  A single cell may contain anywhere from one to hundreds of Golgi stacks.

Ribosome
The protein factory
Structure & Function
•  Composed of two subunits — one large, one small
— made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins.
•  Reads the genetic code carried by messenger RNA
(mRNA) and translates it into a chain of amino acids.
•  Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules deliver the correct
amino acids in the order specified by the mRNA
sequence.
•  Found free-floating in the cytoplasm or attached to
the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
•  Not membrane-bound — technically not a true
organelle by some definitions, but essential all the
same.
Quick Facts
•  A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes.
•  Found in every domain of life — bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes — a sign of their ancient origin.

Lysosome
The recycling and waste center
Structure & Function
•  A membrane-bound sac filled with roughly 40-50
different digestive enzymes.
•  Breaks down worn-out organelles, food particles,
and foreign invaders like bacteria.
•  Maintains an acidic internal environment (around pH
4.5) that activates its enzymes.
•  Plays a role in programmed cell death (apoptosis)
by releasing enzymes when triggered.
•  Recycles cellular building blocks — sugars, amino
acids, and nucleotides — back into the cytoplasm for
reuse.
Quick Facts
•  Sometimes called "suicide bags" because of their role in breaking down cell components.
•  Several genetic disorders (lysosomal storage diseases) result from missing or faulty lysosomal
enzymes.

Chloroplast
The solar power plant of plant cells
Structure & Function
•  Found in plant and algal cells; enclosed by a double
membrane.
•  Contains stacks of disc-shaped membranes called
thylakoids, grouped into stacks called grana.
•  Thylakoid membranes hold chlorophyll, the pigment
that captures light energy and gives plants their green
color.
•  Site of photosynthesis — converting light energy,
water, and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.
•  The fluid surrounding the thylakoids, the stroma, is
where sugar-building reactions (the Calvin cycle)
occur.
Quick Facts
•  Like mitochondria, chloroplasts have their own DNA and likely arose from ancient photosynthetic
bacteria.
•  A single leaf cell can contain 30–50 chloroplasts.

Plasma (Cell) Membrane
The gatekeeper of the cell
Structure & Function
•  Built from a phospholipid bilayer — two layers of
fat molecules with water-loving heads and
water-fearing tails.
•  Selectively permeable: controls what enters and
exits the cell.
•  Embedded membrane proteins act as channels,
pumps, receptors, and identification markers.
•  Cholesterol molecules woven throughout help
maintain membrane flexibility and stability.
•  Described by the fluid mosaic model —
components can drift and move within the layer.
Quick Facts
•  Roughly 5–10 nanometers thick — thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
•  Present in every living cell, from bacteria to humans.

Cytoskeleton
The scaffolding and transport network
Structure & Function
•  A dynamic internal framework of protein filaments
giving the cell shape, strength, and organization.
•  Microtubules (thick, blue) act as tracks for organelle
transport and form the mitotic spindle during division.
•  Microfilaments / actin filaments (thin, red) support
cell shape and enable movement and muscle
contraction.
•  Intermediate filaments (green) provide mechanical
strength and anchor the nucleus and other organelles
in place.
•  Constantly assembles and disassembles to allow the
cell to change shape, divide, and move.
Quick Facts
•  Microtubules are built from a protein called tubulin; microfilaments from actin.
•  Motor proteins like kinesin and myosin "walk" along these filaments to transport cargo.

Centrioles
The organizers of cell division
Structure & Function
•  Two cylindrical structures, arranged at right angles to
each other, forming the centrosome.
•  Each centriole is built from nine triplets of
microtubules arranged in a ring.
•  Organize the mitotic spindle, which pulls
chromosomes apart during cell division.
•  Also give rise to the basal bodies that anchor cilia
and flagella.
•  Duplicate once per cell cycle so each daughter cell
inherits its own pair.
Quick Facts
•  Absent in most plant cells and many fungi, which organize spindles differently.
•  First described in the late 1800s using early light microscopy.

Vacuole
The storage tank of the cell
Structure & Function
•  A large, fluid-filled sac enclosed by a single
membrane called the tonoplast.
•  In plant cells, a central vacuole can occupy up to
90% of the cell's volume.
•  Stores water, nutrients, ions, and waste products;
helps maintain internal pressure (turgor) that keeps
plants rigid.
•  In animal cells, smaller vacuoles assist with storage,
waste removal, and osmotic regulation.
•  In some protists, contractile vacuoles actively pump
out excess water to prevent bursting.
Quick Facts
•  Turgor pressure from the central vacuole is what keeps a healthy plant standing upright.
•  When a plant wilts, its vacuoles have lost much of their water.
